title: Nationalism
competency: List the major factors for the growth of nationalism and discuss how it changed between the 1880s and 1914.

keywords.def: A political force rooted in a shared regional and cultural identity (custom, language, religion); loyalty to one's nation.
A pseudo-science saying history is a struggle of nations for power and survival, which the strongest win.
The lower middle class: small traders, clerks, teachers and officials.
Absorbing newcomers so that they take on the identity of their new nation.

en.text: Nationalism, rooted in a shared regional and cultural identity expressed in custom, language and religion, was the most powerful political force in the West from the 1850s, stronger in towns than among rural peasants. It grew through compulsory primary education and military service, nationalist newspapers and literature, patriotic societies, wars of unification, liberation and colonial expansion, and the pseudo-science of Social Darwinism. It helped make World War I possible.

screens.title: Town or village?
screens.ask: Around 1900, who was more likely to read a nationalist newspaper: a town clerk or a farmer in a far village?
screens.after: Nationalism influenced town people more than rural peasants.

screens.title: What nationalism is
paras: From the 1850s it was the most powerful political force in the West.
Its deepest roots: a shared regional and cultural identity.
This identity shows in custom, language and religion.
It influenced all classes, but town people more than rural peasants.
It grew stronger from the 1850s until World War I.
It worsened the international crisis of 1905–1914.
It made Europeans support the war in July–August 1914.

screens.title: What made it grow
paras: Compulsory primary education taught patriotism.
Compulsory military service built loyalty to the state and ruler.
Cheap newspapers for the masses were often chauvinistic.
"Quality" newspapers were also hostile to neighbours.
Nationalist literature warned of neighbouring countries.
Patriotic societies pushed for more arms and colonies.

screens.title: Wars and "Social Darwinism"
paras: Wars of unification in Italy and Germany stirred nationalism.
So did wars of national liberation in the Balkans.
Britain: frequent small colonial wars.
But the second Boer War (1899–1902) was a shock that cooled British aggressiveness.
USA: victory in the Spanish-American War of 1898.
"Social Darwinism" was a pseudo-science.
It said history is a struggle of nations for power and survival.
The strongest win; the weak are subjugated or destroyed.

screens.text: Why did nationalism influence town people more than peasants?
opts: Schools, newspapers and patriotic societies were concentrated in towns
Villages were ruled by foreign kings
screens.ans: Schools, newspapers and patriotic societies were concentrated in towns
screens.why: The channels of nationalism reached towns first; peasants were more isolated and their loyalties local.

screens.text: The second Boer War made British nationalism more aggressive for a time.
screens.why: p.10: it was an unpleasant shock that cooled British aggressiveness until fear of Germany revived it.
screens.clue: Was it a victory or a shock?

screens.text: How could "Social Darwinism" help make World War I possible?
opts: It taught that war between nations was natural and inevitable
It taught that all nations are equal
screens.ans: It taught that war between nations was natural and inevitable
screens.why: If war is a natural struggle for survival, people accept it and support it when it comes (1914).
screens.clue: Step 1: what did it say about nations? Step 2: how would people then see war?

en.text: Between the 1880s and 1914 nationalism changed: many more, smaller national movements appeared, so it moved from unity to fragmentation; language and ethnicity became the main criteria; and the national question entered the domestic politics of multinational states such as Austria-Hungary and Russia, and Britain with Ireland. The petty bourgeoisie backed minority movements, which promised prestige and public jobs. For governments nationalism was a two-edged weapon. The USA, by contrast, assimilated millions of immigrants.

screens.title: Unity or break-up?
screens.ask: Earlier, nationalism joined small states into Italy and Germany. Later, many small peoples wanted their own states. What would this do to big empires?

screens.title: Three changes
paras: 1. More national movements appeared, in Europe and the Ottoman Empire.
Many were small peoples in small territories.
So nationalism moved from unity to fragmentation.
2. Language and ethnicity became the main criteria, above all language.
Minority peoples demanded equal rights for their languages.
3. The national question entered domestic politics.
Examples: Austria-Hungary, Tsarist Russia, and Britain's Irish question.

screens.title: Who gained, and a two-edged weapon
paras: The petty bourgeoisie backed minority movements.
If their language won, they gained prestige and public-sector jobs.
For governments, nationalism was a two-edged weapon.
It built loyalty and drew workers away from socialism.
But national minorities could turn it into discontent and disloyalty.

screens.title: The USA: a success story
paras: The USA assimilated millions of European emigrants.
They had left Europe unhappy with conditions at home.
As US citizens they gained more economic opportunity.
They also gained more social and political freedom.
